title: Dalgona Candy from Squid Game: Where to Buy It in Seoul (Nov 2026)
keyword: dalgona candy squid game where to buy
content:
📅 Updated 2026.11.19

So, you watched Squid Game, probably binge-watched it in one sitting like most of the world did, and now you’re planning a trip to Korea. Naturally, you’re thinking, “Okay, where can I get my hands on that dalgona candy from Squid Game? Where to buy it?” It's a question I hear a lot from foreign friends visiting Seoul. As of November 18, 2026, the short answer is: it’s not really a common item you'll find just anywhere anymore, but you definitely can still find it if you know where to look – or better yet, make it yourself.

The Reality of Dalgona Candy in Seoul Today (as of November 2026)

Let's be honest right upfront: dalgona (달고나), or ppopgi (뽑기) as it's often called by older Koreans, isn't a mainstream snack you'll grab from a convenience store shelf today. When Squid Game exploded onto the global scene a few years back, there was a massive resurgence of interest. Suddenly, every street corner seemed to have a dalgona vendor, and even some cafes were trying to capitalize on the trend. My office colleagues and I had a brief moment of shared nostalgia, reminiscing about our childhood days trying to perfectly extract the shapes without breaking them. It was fun for a bit, a real blast from the past for us locals. But like many hyper-specific trends, that intense local fever cooled down pretty quickly.

For Koreans, dalgona has always been more of a childhood memory, a street food curiosity you’d stumble upon, rather than a regular craving. It's a simple, brittle sugar candy, often made with baking soda, giving it that distinct slightly bitter, caramelized taste and airy texture. The magic was in the game – picking the shape out with a needle – which Squid Game perfectly captured. Now, in late 2026, the local hype has largely subsided. Most Koreans aren't actively seeking out dalgona candy for their daily snack. It's returned to its pre-Squid Game status: a nostalgic treat, often enjoyed more by the older generation or presented as a retro experience. This is crucial context for foreigners who might arrive expecting to see dalgona stalls on every block, like they would find tteokbokki (spicy rice cakes) or kimbap (seaweed rice rolls). It's not that widespread. It’s definitely shifted to being an attraction primarily for visitors keen to experience a piece of K-drama history.

Point: For locals, dalgona is more a memory than a current craving; its major revival was short-lived here.

Where Foreigners Actually Buy Dalgona Candy: Tourist Spots & Experiences

So, if you're a foreigner searching for "dalgona candy Squid Game where to buy" in Seoul, your best bet is to head directly to the city's major tourist hubs. This is where the demand for such nostalgic experiences is highest, and where vendors cater specifically to visitors. Think places like Myeongdong, Insadong, and occasionally the areas immediately surrounding popular palaces like Gyeongbokgung.

In these spots, you'll likely find small, mobile street stalls or carts run by individual vendors. They'll have a portable burner, a ladle, and all the tools to make dalgona fresh on the spot. This is the authentic experience, complete with the sweet, slightly smoky smell of caramelizing sugar filling the air. You’ll usually see a selection of metal cookie cutters – stars, circles, triangles, umbrellas – just like in the show. The cost for a single dalgona candy typically ranges from 3,000 to 5,000 won (roughly $2.50 to $4 USD), depending on the size and the location. Some vendors might even offer you the 'game' with a toothpick, just like in Squid Game, adding to the fun. The last time I saw a truly bustling dalgona stall was near Gyeongbokgung Palace when I was walking with an overseas friend. The vendor even offered the 'game,' and my friend loved it, clearly delighted to try a piece of the show in real life. These stalls are usually quite visible, often attracting small crowds, so keep an eye out for them, especially during peak tourist hours in the afternoon and evening. They’re not permanent fixtures like a storefront, but pop-up experiences.

Point: Expect to find dalgona candy where tourists gather, made fresh on demand, often with the 'game' included.

Why It's Hard to Just "Buy" Dalgona Like Other Snacks

Many foreigners misunderstand why dalgona isn't just sitting on a shelf in every convenience store or supermarket like a bag of chips. The core reason is simple chemistry: dalgona (whether you call it ppopgi or dalgona) is extremely delicate and sensitive to humidity. It's essentially caramelized sugar that's been aerated with baking soda. This process makes it light and crispy, but also highly hygroscopic, meaning it absorbs moisture from the air very quickly.

Once exposed to humidity, it transforms from a brittle, snap-able treat into a sticky, chewy, and frankly, unappetizing mess. It loses its signature crunch and the ability to be easily carved. This ephemeral nature means it’s just not practical for mass production, packaging, and long-term storage or distribution. Unlike processed snacks with preservatives and airtight packaging, dalgona needs to be eaten almost immediately after it's made. I tried making it once at home after watching a YouTube video, and let me tell you, it went from perfectly crispy to a sticky mess in about twenty minutes in my humid apartment. That’s why you don’t see it on supermarket shelves.

Another point of confusion for many foreigners is the distinction between "dalgona candy" and "dalgona coffee." While both use the word "dalgona," they are completely different things. Dalgona coffee is the whipped coffee trend that also went viral during the pandemic – essentially instant coffee, sugar, and hot water whipped into a frothy topping for milk. It gets its name because its fluffy, caramel-colored texture resembles the appearance of the candy, but it contains no actual dalgona candy. Squid Game specifically featured the candy, not the coffee. So, if you're looking for the Squid Game experience, make sure you're asking for the candy!

Point: Dalgona's delicate, humidity-sensitive nature makes it unsuitable for mass retail, requiring it to be made and consumed fresh.

Your Best Bet: DIY Dalgona Candy (It's Easier Than You Think)

If you're not planning to spend all your time in tourist hotspots, or if you simply want a more hands-on and consistent way to enjoy dalgona candy, then making it yourself is absolutely your best option. It's surprisingly simple, incredibly fun, and gives you bragging rights – plus, you can play the Squid Game challenge as many times as you want!

All you really need are two basic ingredients: sugar and baking soda. The tools are also quite simple: a ladle (preferably one with a long handle), a small heat source (a gas burner works best), a flat non-stick surface (like parchment paper or a greased metal plate), and something flat to press the hot sugar down. And, of course, your choice of metal cookie cutters for the shapes. You can find comprehensive "dalgona candy making kits" easily online, both on global e-commerce platforms and on Korean sites like Coupang (쿠팡/Kupang), which deliver quickly here. These kits typically include everything you need, from ladles to shape cutters and the pressing tool.

A coworker at my company recently bought a small dalgona making kit online for his kids. He said it was surprisingly fun, and way cheaper than buying one-off candies from a street vendor. He even brought a perfectly molded star to the office one morning to show off! It’s also a fantastic souvenir idea if you want to bring a piece of Korean culture back home to share with friends and family. The instructions are usually straightforward, and there are countless YouTube tutorials that walk you through the process step-by-step. The key is to work quickly once the sugar is melted and the baking soda is mixed in, as it hardens very fast.

Point: For consistent access, creative fun, and an authentic experience, making your own dalgona candy is the most practical and enjoyable approach.

Beyond the Candy: Dalgona's Cultural Footprint Today

Even if the direct hunt for "dalgona candy Squid Game where to buy" leads you mostly to tourist areas or DIY projects, the cultural impact of dalgona goes deeper. While the candy itself has returned to its niche, the idea of dalgona – its aesthetic, its nostalgic appeal – lives on, particularly within Korea's robust "new-tro" (뉴트로/new-tro) trend.

New-tro is a portmanteau of "new" and "retro," and it's a huge deal here. It’s where younger generations embrace and reinterpret retro styles, aesthetics, and even flavors from the 70s, 80s, and 90s. Dalgona candy, with its simple, almost crude charm, fits perfectly into this movement. You'll see new-tro influences in cafes designed with old-school signage, fashion that reintroduces vintage silhouettes, and even in music and art. Dalgona, even if not physically present, symbolizes this yearning for a simpler, more analog past. Sometimes when I grab a coffee with my colleagues, someone will jokingly ask if I want 'dalgona coffee' even though we're talking about the whipped coffee, not the candy, showing how deeply the word entered the common lexicon. It’s a shorthand for a certain kind of nostalgic, unpretentious fun. So while you might not easily find the actual candy in every corner shop as of November 2026, its spirit, and its connection to Korean retro culture, remains strong.

Point: Dalgona's legacy is more about its nostalgic cultural symbol within the new-tro trend and its name in coffee, rather than a widely available everyday snack.
summary: While the Squid Game dalgona candy isn't a ubiquitous snack in Korea as of November 2026, it remains a popular tourist experience found in specific street stalls. For a more reliable and fun experience, making dalgona yourself with a simple kit is highly recommended.
